paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome is a clinically variable and genetically heterogeneous disorder with eye, joint, orofacial, and hearing features. It can be inherited in an autosomal dominant or an autosomal recessive pattern (Faletra et al., 2014). Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive form caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in COL9A3 (Rad et al., 2022). In a review of 7 families, Rad et al. (2022) found that moderate to profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate to high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration were consistent features. Retinal detachment and cataract occurred only occasionally, and skeletal involvement varied.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) described a boy (International Skeletal Dysplasia Registry R08-308A) of Indian origin with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. He failed his newborn hearing screen. At 5 months he had moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe sensorineural hearing loss on the left, and the hearing loss remained stable. Temporal bone CT showed mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months. By 2 years he had myopia of -6.75 OD and -8 OS, and this had progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. No vitreous abnormalities were noted. He had femoral and tibial bowing at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed flattened acetabula, slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly with irregularities of the vertebral endplates. He also had midfacial hypoplasia. He did not have cleft palate or pes planus. Growth, gross motor development, and intelligence were normal. Early speech delay was attributed to his hearing loss.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome born to healthy nonconsanguineous Russian parents. At 1 month he had adductor spasm, hip dysplasia, and bilateral absence of ossification centers. Congenital bilateral high myopia was found at 3 months, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss of grade 3-4 was diagnosed at 11 months. Speech was delayed, but motor development was normal. Radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, with spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae, mild platyspondyly, kyphosis, flattened and irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. Eye examination showed peripheral pigment rearrangement, multiple vitreous floaters, and a preretinal membrane, with a normal ERG. At 2 years 5 months he had genu valgum, waddling gait, and pain in the lower limb joints. He also had a flattened nasal bridge, a small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, a high palate, lumbar lordosis, long fingers, and planovalgus feet. His height was in the normal range.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) described a 28-year-old Iranian woman (family 1) who was the only affected child of first-cousin parents. She had high myopia in both eyes and vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, and retinal pigmentary changes. She also had severe, progressive sensorineural hearing loss and unilateral absence of the frontal sinus. Her joints and bones were normal on x-ray and examination, although she had knee pain. She did not have the typical Stickler craniofacial features (midface hypoplasia, cleft palate, micrognathia, depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares). Her height was 157 cm (-0.8 SD).

Neither the parents nor the older sister had reported hearing loss, myopia, or skeletal anomalies, and all 3 were heterozygous for the COL9A3 mutation, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: In a Russian boy with Stickler syndrome, Markova et al. (2021) identified compound heterozygosity for a c.268C-T transition in exon 5 of the COL9A3 gene, resulting in an arg90-to-ter (R90X) substitution, and a c.1729C-T transition resulting in an R577X substitution. The mutations were found by targeted sequencing of 166 skeletal disorder genes and were shown to be in trans by Sanger sequencing of the family. The healthy sibs did not carry pathogenic COL9A3 variants.
